html:
The Celtiberians were Celtic-speaking peoples of the central and northeastern Iberian Peninsula, in the uplands of what is now Spain, in the last centuries BCE. The map places the label as early as 1500 BCE, long before they are known; their culture is clear in the archaeology from about the 600s BCE.

They mixed traditions. They spoke a Celtic language but wrote it in a script borrowed from their neighbours the Iberians. They lived in hillforts and towns, herded and farmed, and were famous as tough fighters and makers of iron swords. Many served as mercenaries for Carthage and later Rome.

Their wars with Rome were long and bitter. The Celtiberian Wars began in 181 BCE and ended with the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE, after a long siege by Scipio Aemilianus starved the town into surrender; many defenders killed themselves first. They fought again for the rebel general Sertorius in the 70s BCE. By 72 BCE the region was firmly part of Roman Hispania, and the Celtiberian language slowly gave way to Latin.
